questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Severity of a crack from its size
questions.learningObjective: Explain how crack size governs the tolerable stress of a part
questions.stem: Rendering note 6 asks the translator to explain in writing why a crack twice as long can be far more dangerous than a short one.

answer.exemplar: The stress intensity near a crack tip scales as K = sigma times the square root of pi a, where sigma is the applied stress and a is the crack length. A material has a fixed toughness K_IC, the largest stress intensity it can tolerate, so the allowable stress is sigma_c = K_IC divided by the square root of pi a. Doubling the crack length therefore lowers the stress the part can carry by a factor of the square root of two, about 1.41, which is why inspection intervals are set by the largest tolerable flaw.

questions.explanation: The stress intensity scales as the square root of the crack length, so the tolerable stress falls as one over the square root of it. Doubling the crack length cuts the safe stress by about 1.41.
questions.hint: Stress intensity goes as the square root of crack size.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Mean square displacement after a time
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the mean square displacement grows in proportion to time
questions.stem: Style note 14 asks the translator to explain in writing why the mean square displacement of a diffusing particle grows in proportion to time.

answer.exemplar: A particle performing random walk steps of length l makes N steps in a time t, and the number of steps grows as N = v t with v the typical speed. The mean square displacement is N times l squared because the cross terms between different steps cancel on averaging. Substitution gives a mean square displacement proportional to t, and the constant of proportionality is the diffusion constant, six times that constant in three dimensions. The spread therefore grows as the square root of time while the mean square grows linearly.

questions.explanation: Random stepping makes the mean square displacement proportional to the number of steps, which grows linearly with time. The rms distance grows with the square root of time, the signature of diffusion.
questions.hint: Mean square follows the step count, rms the root.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Minority carrier population in doped material
questions.learningObjective: Explain why heavier doping reduces the minority carrier population
questions.stem: Session note 33 asks the translator to explain in writing why a heavily doped sample has fewer minority carriers than a lightly doped one.

answer.exemplar: In a doped semiconductor the product of the majority and minority carrier densities is fixed at the square of the intrinsic carrier density, a result called mass action. If a sample is doped n-type with a donor density N_D, the holes are the minority carriers and their density is p = n_i squared divided by N_D. Raising the donor density therefore lowers the minority hole density in inverse proportion, and the same relation holds with the roles exchanged for p-type material. This is why minority carrier lifetimes dominate the behaviour of diodes and of the base region of a bipolar transistor.

questions.explanation: Mass action fixes the product of the majority and minority densities at the square of the intrinsic density, so ten times more doping means ten times fewer minority carriers. Ignoring that relation misses the effect.
questions.hint: Mass action links the two carrier densities.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Stiffness from a measured stress and strain
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a stiffness value is extracted from a tensile test
questions.stem: Q and A 16 asks the translator to explain in writing how the stiffness of a rod is obtained from a stress and a strain measurement.

answer.exemplar: The stress is the force divided by the cross sectional area, and the strain is the fractional change in length, that is the extension divided by the original length. Their ratio, stress over strain, is Young's modulus, a measure of the resistance of the material to elastic deformation measured in pascals. Because both stress and strain are geometric quantities that refer to the sample itself, the modulus depends on the material rather than on the dimensions of the rod, whereas the spring constant of the rod does depend on its length and cross section.

questions.explanation: Young's modulus is stress divided by strain, and both are computed for the sample measured. The value characterises the material, whereas the spring constant of a rod also depends on its length and cross section.
questions.hint: Stress over strain for the sample.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Diffusion constant of a small molecule
questions.learningObjective: Explain how temperature and viscosity set the diffusion constant
questions.stem: Closing note 44 asks the translator to write out how the diffusion constant of a molecule in a liquid changes with temperature and why.

answer.exemplar: The Stokes-Einstein relation D = kT over 6 pi eta r expresses the diffusion constant of a spherical solute as the product of the Boltzmann constant and the absolute temperature in the numerator, divided by 6 pi times the viscosity of the liquid and the radius of the solute. The numerator grows slowly and linearly with the absolute temperature, while the viscosity of a liquid falls steeply as the temperature rises because the thermal motion of the molecules weakens their grip on one another. The net effect is that heating a liquid speeds up diffusion strongly, unlike diffusion in a gas.

questions.explanation: Stokes-Einstein makes the diffusion constant proportional to temperature and inversely proportional to viscosity, and viscosity falls sharply as a liquid warms. Both effects therefore speed up diffusion.
questions.hint: Temperature rises, viscosity falls.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Stiffness from a measured stress and strain
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a modulus does not depend on the size of the sample
questions.stem: Explanation note 55 asks the translator to explain in writing why the Young's modulus of a metal does not depend on the size of the sample tested.

answer.exemplar: Young's modulus is defined as stress divided by strain. Stress is the applied force divided by the cross sectional area, and strain is the extension divided by the original length. Both quantities are normalised by the geometry of the sample, so the ratio measures only how the material resists deformation. A thicker rod carries a proportionally larger force for the same stress and stretches by the same fraction, which is why the modulus is the same for a thick bar and a thin wire of the same alloy. The spring constant of the rod, in contrast, does depend on its length and cross section.

questions.explanation: Stress and strain are both normalised by the sample geometry, so their ratio is a material property. The spring constant of a particular rod does depend on its length and cross section, which is a different quantity.
questions.hint: Both stress and strain are normalised.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Minority carrier population in doped material
questions.learningObjective: Explain why minority carriers control the reverse current of a junction
questions.stem: Annotation 34 asks the translator to explain in writing why the minority carriers rather than the majority carriers control the current in a reverse biased junction.

answer.exemplar: The reverse current of a junction is carried by minority carriers, which are thermally generated within the depletion region and must diffuse across it. The density of these carriers is set by mass action, so in a strongly doped sample the minority density is very small, of the order of the intrinsic density squared over the doping density. Because this population is tiny, the reverse current saturates at a low value set by the generation rate rather than by the applied voltage. In forward bias the barrier is reduced and the large majority population floods the junction, giving a large rectification ratio.

questions.explanation: The reverse current is carried by thermally generated minority carriers, whose density is set by mass action and is tiny in a doped sample. The reverse current saturates, while forward bias uncovers the large majority population.
questions.hint: Reverse current rides on minority carriers.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Diffusion constant of a small molecule
questions.learningObjective: Explain why molecules of similar mass can diffuse at different rates
questions.stem: Retouch note 7 asks the translator to write out why two molecules of similar mass can have very different diffusion constants in the same liquid.

answer.exemplar: The Stokes-Einstein relation D = kT over 6 pi eta r makes the diffusion constant depend on the radius of the moving molecule, not only on its mass. A compact molecule of the same mass presents a small hydrodynamic radius and meets less viscous drag, while an elongated molecule of the same mass presents a large radius and is slowed more strongly by the solvent. Since the drag grows with the radius and the diffusion constant falls as one over that radius, molecules of identical mass can differ in diffusion constant by a large factor. This is why globular proteins diffuse far faster than elongated molecules of comparable mass in the same solvent.

questions.explanation: Stokes-Einstein makes the diffusion constant inversely proportional to the hydrodynamic radius, so shape matters even at fixed mass. Treating mass as the only control would wrongly predict identical constants.
questions.hint: The radius, not the mass, sets the drag.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Conductivity of a doped semiconductor
questions.learningObjective: Explain how doping and mobility together set semiconductor conductivity
questions.stem: Nomenclature note 18 asks the translator to explain in writing how the conductivity of a semiconductor changes when it is doped and how the mobility enters.

answer.exemplar: The conductivity of a semiconductor is the sum of two carrier contributions, q N_D mu_n for the electrons and q N_A mu_p for the holes. In an n-type sample the donors supply a large electron population while the hole population is set by mass action and is tiny, so the electron term dominates and the conductivity rises steeply with the donor density. The mobility appears as a factor because it sets how far a carrier travels under a given field, and it is limited by scattering from the lattice and from the dopant atoms themselves, which is why a heavily doped sample has a slightly lower mobility as well.

questions.explanation: Conductivity combines charge, carrier density and mobility for each carrier type, and doping raises the majority carrier density enormously. Mobility enters too, and it falls slightly in heavily doped material.
questions.hint: Charge times density times mobility, summed.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the square root scaling of a polymer coil size
questions.stem: Wrap note 47 asks the translator to explain in writing why the size of a polymer coil depends on the square root of the number of links.

answer.exemplar: In a freely jointed chain each link points in an independent random direction, so the end to end vector is the sum of N random vectors of length l. Because the directions are random, the cross terms in the square of that sum average to zero, leaving a mean square distance of N times l squared. The root mean square distance is therefore l times the square root of N, so quadrupling the number of links doubles the size of the coil. A fully stretched chain of length N l is far longer than this random coil, and the ratio between the two grows without bound as the chain gets longer.

questions.explanation: Random link directions cancel the cross terms, leaving a mean square distance of N l squared and a coil size of l times the root of N. The stretched length N l grows linearly, so the two diverge for long chains.
questions.hint: Cross terms cancel in a random coil.

questions.topic: Diffusion constant of a small molecule
questions.learningObjective: Compare a diffusion constant at two temperatures
questions.stem: Voice note 29 asks first for the diffusion constant of a solute of radius 0.20 nm in water of viscosity 1.0e-3 pascal seconds at 300 K and then for the value at 330 K.

options.text: The constant is 1.10e-9 at 300 K and 1.10e-9 square metres per second at 330 K.
options.misconception: believes the diffusion constant has no temperature dependence

options.text: The constant is 1.10e-9 at 300 K and 1.21e-9 square metres per second at 330 K.
The constant is 2.20e-9 at 300 K and 2.42e-9 square metres per second at 330 K.
options.misconception: forgets the factor of one half in the Stokes-Einstein numerator

options.text: The constant is 1.10e-9 at 300 K and 0.91e-9 square metres per second at 330 K.
options.misconception: assumes the diffusion constant falls as the liquid warms

questions.explanation: Stokes-Einstein gives 1.099e-9 square metres per second at 300 K and 1.209e-9 at 330 K, since only kT changes when the viscosity is fixed. Halving or doubling the value miscounts a factor.
questions.hint: Only kT changes between the two temperatures.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Mean square displacement after a time
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the rms distance from the mean square displacement
questions.stem: Legend entry 49 asks how the rms distance of a diffusing particle compares with the mean square displacement.

options.text: The rms distance equals the mean square displacement, since both describe the spread of the particle.
options.misconception: treats the rms distance and the mean square displacement as the same quantity

options.text: The rms distance is the square of the mean square displacement, since spreading accelerates with time.
options.misconception: squares the mean square displacement to reach the rms distance

options.text: The rms distance is the square root of the mean square displacement, so it grows as the square root of time.
The rms distance grows in direct proportion to time, while the mean square displacement grows with the square root of time.
options.misconception: swaps the time dependences of the rms distance and the mean square

questions.explanation: The rms distance is the square root of the mean square displacement, so with a mean square proportional to time the rms distance grows as the square root of time. Swapping the powers reverses the spreading law.
questions.hint: The rms distance is the root of the mean square.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Size of a freely jointed chain
questions.learningObjective: Match tabulated coil sizes to the freely jointed chain formula
questions.stem: Deck note 17 tabulates the rms end to end distances of three freely jointed chains: 3.2 nm for 100 links of 0.32 nm, 5.7 nm for 320 links of 0.32 nm, and 10.1 nm for 1000 links of 0.32 nm.

options.text: Each distance equals the link length times the link count, so the coil size grows in direct proportion to N.
options.misconception: treats the coil as if it were fully stretched

options.text: Each distance is independent of the link count, so the coil size is fixed by the link length alone.
options.misconception: believes the coil size does not depend on chain length

options.text: Each distance equals the link count times the square of the link length, so the coil size grows as N.
options.misconception: confuses the mean square distance with the rms distance

options.text: Each distance equals the link length times the square root of the link count, so the coil size grows as the root of N.

questions.explanation: Multiplying 0.32 nm by the square root of the link counts gives 3.2, 5.72 and 10.12 nm, matching the table, so the coil size follows a root of N law. A stretched chain would be far longer.
questions.hint: Try the link length times the root of N.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Stiffness from a measured stress and strain
questions.learningObjective: Compute a stiffness value from a bar test
questions.stem: Galley note 6 gives a bar of cross section 2.0e-5 square metres that stretches 0.00040 m under a load of 2.0e3 N over an original length of 0.200 m, and asks for the stiffness.
questions.explanation: The stress is 1.0e8 pascals and the strain is 0.00040 over 0.200, that is 0.002, so the modulus is 5.0e10 pascals. Using the extension instead of the strain overstates it fiftyfold.
questions.hint: Modulus is stress over strain.
